blocks.text: The Philosopher (Hist. book 8, ch. 12) writes that cranes migrate from Thrace τοῦ Μαιμακτηριῶνος [tou Maimaktēriōnos], in the month Maemacterion; and Aelian, book 3, ch. 13, Φθινοπώρου ἤδη μεσοῦντος [Phthinopōrou ēdē mesountos], in mid-autumn. This strongly confirms what Scaliger maintained against Gaza, and Samuel Petit against Petavius in his Eclogae chronologicae, book 4: that among the Attic months Maemacterion is not the first but the second of the autumn months. Aelian defines the time of their return thus: Ὅταν ὑπεύδια ἄρξηται, καὶ εἰρηναῖα τοῦ ἀέρος ὑποστρέφουσιν ὀπίσω [Hotan hypeudia arxētai, kai eirēnaia tou aeros hypostrephousin opisō]; when the fair weather begins and the calm of the air [II, 628] returns, they come back. And Maximus of Tyre: Αἱ γέρανοι ἐξ Αἰγύπτου ὥραθέρους ἀφισάμεναι, οὐκ ἀνεχόμεναι τὸ θάλπος, τείνασαι πτέρυγας ὥσπερ ἱςία, φέρονται διὰ τοῦ ἀέρος εὐθὺ τῶν Σκυθῶν γῆς [Hai geranoi ex Aigyptou hōratherous aphisamenai, ouk anechomenai to thalpos, teinasai pterygas hōsper histia, pherontai dia tou aeros euthy tōn Skythōn gēs]; The cranes, departing from Egypt in summer because they cannot endure the heat, spread their wings like sails and are carried straight through the air to the Scythian region. Accordingly Pliny calls them summer visitors. I take this in such a way that under the name of summer I also understand spring. On these lines of Theocritus, Idyll 10,
Ἁ αἶξ τὸν κύτισον, ὁ λύκος τὰν αἶγα διώκει, Ἁ γέρανος τ᾽ ὤροτρον, — — — [Ha aix ton kytison, ho lykos tan aiga diōkei, Ha geranos t᾽ ōrotron]

The goat follows the clover, the wolf the goat, the crane the plough, the Scholiast says: Ἀρχομένου γὰρ σπόρου αἱ γέρανοι φαίνονται [Archomenou gar sporou hai geranoi phainontai], For cranes appear at the beginning of sowing. This I do not understand, since cranes do not arrive at sowing time but depart. For the migration of cranes falls in autumn, which is the customary time of sowing. Virgil, Georgics book 1:
When Libra has made the hours of day and sleep equal, and now divides the globe in the middle between light and shade, work your bulls, men, sow barley in the fields.

On these words Servius says: He says that grain is to be sown in the autumn season. So the Greekling who wrote these Scholia is talking nonsense. Aristophanes is therefore διαῤῥήδην [diarrhēdēn] opposed to him. For in the Birds he bids us
Σπείρειν μὲν ὅταν γέρανος κρώζουσ᾽ ἐς τὴν Λιβύην μεταχωρῇ, [Speirein men hotan geranos krōzous᾽ es tēn Libyēn metachōrē]
Sow when the crane migrates, crying, to Libya. The Scholiast notes that this is taken from Hesiod's Works, line 446:

Φράζεσθαι δ᾽ εὖ τ᾽ ἂν φωνὴν γεράνου ἐπακούσης, Ὑψόθεν ἐκ νεφέων ἐνιαύσια κεκληγυίης, Ἡτ᾽ ἀρότοιό τε σῆμα φέρει, καὶ χείματος ὥρην Δεικνύει ὀμβρηροῦ· — — — [Phrazesthai d᾽ eu t᾽ an phōnēn geranou epakousēs, Hypsothen ek nepheōn eniausia keklēgyiēs, Hēt᾽ arotoio te sēma pherei, kai cheimatos hōrēn Deiknyei ombrērou]
Take heed when you hear the voice of the migrating crane, crying every year from on high in the clouds, which gives the signal for ploughing and shows the season of rainy winter.

From what has been said about the migration of cranes it is clear that the Prophet not without reason sets them forth as an example of natural prudence. The swallow, he says, and the crane have kept the time of their coming; but my people has not known the judgment of the Lord. Accordingly the Philosopher (Hist. book 9, ch. 10) begins his account of the migration of cranes thus: Φρόνιμα δὲ πολλὰ καὶ περὶ τὰς γεράνους δοκεῖ συμβαίνειν [Phronima de polla kai peri tas geranous dokei symbainein]; Many things also seem to be done prudently by cranes. And Aelian, History book 3, chapter 14, maintains that men learned τὸ κυβερνητικὸν [to kybernētikon], the art of steering, from them. And Cassiodorus holds that Mercury, [II, 629] Philostratus that Palamedes, had cranes as teachers. Accordingly among the Egyptians, as Horus reports, a watchful crane signified a cautious man, and a flying crane ἄνθρωπον εἰδότα τὰ μετέωρα [anthrōpon eidota ta meteōra], a man skilled in lofty matters. [col. 79] And among the Arabs one who is very cautious is called, in a common proverb, احرس من الكركي [aḥras min al-kurkī], more cautious than a crane.

Nor should anyone wonder that the crane is among the clean birds rather than the stork, a bird very like it, since the stork feeds on serpents, the crane on crops and seeds. An old author in Suidas: Γέρανοι γεωργοῦ κατενέμοντο χώραν ἐσπαρμένην νεωστὶ πυρίνῳ σίτῳ [Geranoi geōrgou katenemonto chōran esparmenēn neōsti pyrinō sitō], Cranes were grazing on a farmer's field newly sown with wheat. Aelian, book 2, ch. 1: Σπείραντας δὲ τοὺς Αἰγυπτίους καταλαμβάνουσι, καὶ τράπεζαν, ὡς ἂν εἴποις, ἄφθονον τὴν ἐν ταῖς ἀρούραις εὑρόντες, εἶτα ἄκλητοι ξενίων μεταλαγχάνουσιν [Speirantas de tous Aigyptious katalambanousi, kai trapezan, hōs an eipois, aphthonon tēn en tais arourais heurontes, eita aklētoi xeniōn metalanchanousin]; They come upon the Egyptians as they are sowing, and finding in the fields a table, so to speak, abounding in food, they enjoy, uninvited, the rights of hospitality. Hence Mela writes that the Pygmies fought against the cranes for their sown crops; and Antipater of Sidon, as cited above, in the Epitaph of a Fowler:
Ὁ πρὶν ἐγὼ καὶ ψῆρα καὶ ἁρπάκτειραν ἐρύκων Σπέρματος ὑψιπετῆ Βιστόνιαν γέρανον. [Ho prin egō kai psēra kai harpakteiran erykōn Spermatos hypsipetē Bistonian geranon]
